lessons.title: When to Hire Your First Employee
lessons.body:
You know it's time to hire when you are turning down orders because you can't produce fast enough, or when you are working so many hours that quality drops. A good rule: if you consistently have more orders than you can fill in a 40-hour week, and your profit after materials is at least 3 times the cost of a helper's daily wage, you can afford to hire. For example, if a helper costs 5,000 shillings per day and your daily profit is 20,000 shillings, you can pay a helper and still keep 15,000 shillings. Start with one person.

In Africa, you can hire casually or formally. For a first employee, many small producers use a casual laborer paid daily or weekly. But if you want reliability, consider a 3-month probation contract. Pay at least the local minimum wageâin Kenya, that's about 15,000 KES per month for a general worker in 2023. You must also budget for NHIF and NSSF if formal. To find someone, ask family, church, or local Facebook groups. Avoid hiring friends unless you can be clear about expectations.

Train your first employee on one specific task: cutting, packing, or operating the rewinding machine. Write down the steps and show them. Check their work for the first week. Pay on time, every time. If they do well, give a small bonus when you meet a big order. This builds loyalty.

Keep records: name, phone, daily attendance, and pay. Use a simple notebook or a free app like Wave or Kobo. When you hire, your role shifts from doing everything to managing. You must now plan, buy materials, and find customers. Don't hire until you have at least 3 months of steady orders. Otherwise, you may have to let them go, which is hard and damages your reputation.

lessons.title: Investing in a Semi-Automatic Rewinding Machine
lessons.body:
A semi-automatic rewinding machine turns large jumbo rolls of tissue paper into finished toilet rolls or kitchen towels. Manual rewinding is slowâabout 50 rolls per hour. A semi-automatic machine can do 200-300 rolls per hour, depending on the model. In Africa, you can buy a used Chinese-made machine for 1.5 to 3 million shillings (about $1,000-$2,000). New ones cost 5-8 million shillings. Look on Alibaba, or check local importers in Nairobi, Lagos, or Johannesburg.

Before buying, calculate payback. If you sell each roll at 30 shillings and your material cost is 15 shillings, you make 15 shillings per roll. To pay back a 2 million shilling machine, you need to sell about 133,000 rolls. At 200 rolls per hour and 5 hours per day, that's 1,000 rolls per day, so 133 daysâabout 4.5 months. That's a good investment.

You also need a compressor (for the machine's air pressure) and a power stabilizer. Most machines run on 3-phase power, but some are single-phase. Check your electricity supply. In areas with frequent outages, a small generator (5-10 KVA) is essential. Budget an extra 300,000 shillings for installation and electrical work.

Where to put it? A dry, secure room at least 3m x 4m. The machine needs a flat floor. Train yourself or a technician on operation and basic maintenance: daily oiling, cleaning the glue rollers, and checking the cutting blade. Keep spare blades and glue. Buy your jumbo rolls from a supplierâoften imported from Egypt or South Africa. Order in bulk to save on transport. With a semi-automatic machine, you can double or triple production without hiring many people.

lessons.title: Increasing Production Without Compromising Quality
lessons.body:
Scaling up doesn't mean letting quality slip. First, standardize your process. Write down every step from receiving jumbo rolls to packing finished products. For toilet paper: check the roll weight (should be 100-120g per roll), the perforation (clean tear), and the wrapper (tight and neat). For kitchen towels: check absorbency and sheet count. Use a simple checklist and train your workers to follow it.

Second, buy better raw materials. Cheaper jumbo rolls may have more breaks or dust. Test a small batch from a new supplier before committing. A good jumbo roll should be consistent in thickness and width. If you switch suppliers, adjust your machine settings. Keep a sample of your best roll as a reference.

Third, invest in quality control. Weigh 10 random rolls every hour. If any are underweight, stop and fix the machine. Keep a logbook. For customers like supermarkets, consistency matters more than perfection. They want every pack to have the same number of rolls and the same look.

Fourth, maintain your equipment. A dull blade causes ragged cuts. A dirty glue roller causes loose wrapping. Schedule maintenance every Friday afternoon: clean, oil, and check. Keep spare parts.

Finally, don't rush. If you increase speed too fast, you'll get more jams and waste. Increase production by 20% each week, not 100%. Monitor wasteâif more than 5% of your rolls are rejected, slow down. Quality builds your brand. A customer who buys a bad pack once may never return. But a customer who trusts your brand will buy again and again, even if your price is slightly higher.

lessons.title: Finding Larger Buyers: Supermarkets and Distributors
lessons.body:
Supermarkets and distributors can buy in bulk, but they demand reliability, packaging, and paperwork. Start by making a list of supermarkets in your town or city. Include local chains like Naivas, Quickmart, or Shoprite, and independent stores. Also list distributors who supply these storesâthey often buy from small producers.

Before approaching them, prepare a professional package. You need: a sample pack of your best products, a price list (per roll, per pack, per bale), and a simple proposal. Your packaging must have a brand name, barcode (you can get one from GS1 Kenya for about 10,000 KES), and contact details. Supermarkets may ask for a certificate of analysis or quality testâyou can get a basic test from KEBS or a private lab for 5,000-15,000 KES.

Call the supermarket's purchasing manager. Ask for a meeting. Be on time, dress neatly, and bring samples. Explain your production capacity: how many rolls per day, your lead time (e.g., 3 days), and your minimum order. Offer a trial: supply 50 packs on consignment (they pay after selling). If they like it, they'll order more.

For distributors, offer a wholesale price that gives them a 20-30% margin. For example, if you sell to a supermarket at 25 shillings per roll, offer distributors at 20 shillings. They will buy in larger volumes. Keep records of every sale. Follow up after delivery to check satisfaction. Ask for feedback on packaging and quality.

Be patient. It may take 2-3 months to get your first supermarket order. But once you do, pay attention to their payment termsâoften 30 days. You may need working capital to cover that gap. Also, be ready to deliver on time. One late delivery can lose the account.

lessons.title: Expanding to New Products: Paper Plates, Cups, and Tissues
lessons.body:
Once your tissue line is stable, you can add paper plates, cups, and facial tissues. These use similar raw materials and machinery. For paper plates, you need a plate-making machine (manual or semi-automatic). A manual machine costs 500,000-1,000,000 shillings and makes 30-50 plates per hour. Semi-automatic: 2-3 million shillings, 200-300 plates per hour. You'll need food-grade paper board (300-400 gsm). Buy from paper suppliers in Nairobi or import from India.

For paper cups, a cup-making machine is more expensive: 3-5 million shillings for a basic model. You also need a cup bottom and side sealing machine. Start with 4oz and 7oz cups for events and water. Raw material is PE-coated paper board. This is a bigger investment, so only expand if you have steady demand from caterers, hotels, or supermarkets.

Facial tissues are easier. You can use the same jumbo rolls but need a folding and cutting machine. A small machine costs 800,000-1,500,000 shillings. Package in 100-sheet boxes or soft packs. Target pharmacies, hotels, and supermarkets.

Before buying any new machine, test the market. Ask 10 potential customers if they would buy your product at your price. For example, if you plan to sell paper plates at 5 shillings each, and local shops sell at 6 shillings, you have a margin. Start small: buy a used machine, produce 100 units, and try to sell them. If they sell within a week, buy more. If not, reconsider.

Expanding product lines spreads your risk. If tissue sales drop, plates may keep you afloat. But don't do everything at once. Master one new product before adding another. Keep separate records for each product to know what's profitable.

lessons.title: Financing Growth: Loans, Savings Groups, and Grants
lessons.body:
To scale up, you need money. The cheapest source is your own savings and reinvested profit. Aim to save 20% of your monthly profit in a separate account. Use a mobile money savings account like M-Shwari or a bank savings account. For a 2 million shilling machine, saving 100,000 shillings per month takes 20 monthsâtoo slow. So consider other options.

Savings groups (chamas, SACCOs, or village banks) are common in Africa. In a chama, 10-20 members contribute monthly. You can borrow 3-5 times your contribution. For example, if you contribute 10,000 shillings monthly for 6 months, you can borrow up to 300,000 shillings. Interest is often 1-2% per month. This is good for buying raw materials or a small machine. Join a chama that focuses on business. Be transparent about your plans.

Bank loans: Many banks in Africa have SME products. In Kenya, KCB, Equity, and Co-operative Bank offer loans from 100,000 to 5 million shillings. You need a business plan, 6 months of bank statements, and collateral (land, vehicle, or savings). Interest rates: 12-18% per year. For a 2 million shilling loan at 15% over 3 years, monthly repayment is about 70,000 shillings. Only borrow if your additional profit from the machine exceeds that.

Grants: Organizations like the African Development Bank, USAID, and local NGOs offer grants for small businesses. Check websites like fundsforNGOs or local business incubators. Grants are competitive and take time. You often need a proposal and reporting. But they don't need repayment. Start by applying for small grants (50,000-200,000 shillings) for equipment.

Avoid loan sharks (shylocks) who charge 20% per month. They will destroy your business. Always compare total cost of borrowing. Keep records of all loans and repayments. Build a good credit historyâpay on time. As you grow, you can negotiate better terms.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Scaling Up Production in African Tissue & Paper Enterprises

Scaling a tissue and paper products business in Africa is rarely about buying the biggest machine available. It is about matching each new cost to a proven revenue stream, then repeating that discipline at every stage. This reference consolidates the practical thresholds, numbers, and decision rules that sit behind the six lessons in this module. Use it as a working document: print it, annotate it, and revisit it each time you consider a hire, a machine, a new buyer, or a loan.

The African context matters. Demand for tissue, serviettes, paper plates, and cups is growing with urbanisation, fast food, hospitality, and institutional buyers such as schools, clinics, and offices. At the same time, small producers face high import costs for jumbo reels, volatile electricity, and limited access to affordable credit. The operators who scale successfully tend to be those who sell before they spend, keep quality consistent while adding volume, and finance growth from a mix of internal cash flow, savings groups, and targeted grants or loans rather than a single large debt.

Decision Thresholds: When Each Step Is Justified

The single most common mistake in this sector is investing ahead of demand. A semi-automatic rewinding machine that sits idle destroys cash flow faster than almost any other error. The thresholds below are drawn from small-manufacturer benchmarks used across East and West Africa and should be treated as minimum triggers, not targets.

Table 1: Scaling decision thresholds for tissue & paper SMEs
Decision Minimum trigger Typical cost (USD) Payback period
Hire first production employee Operating â¥ 60% of single-shift capacity for 3 consecutive months; owner working > 60 hrs/week 60â150/month (varies by country) Immediate (frees owner for sales)
Semi-automatic rewinding machine Consistent orders exceeding manual capacity; 3+ months of unmet demand 2,500â8,000 8â18 months
Second delivery vehicle / larger stock Signed supply agreement with a distributor or supermarket chain 1,500â5,000 12â24 months
New product line (plates, cups) Core tissue line profitable for 12+ months; existing buyers requesting the new product 3,000â15,000 18â36 months
Formal loan or grant application Documented 6-month sales records; clear use-of-funds tied to a signed order or contract Varies Match to asset life

Sources: Cost ranges compiled from ILO (2020) Growing Your Business; AfDB (2022) Africa SME Programme; and TechnoServe small-manufacturer cost benchmarks for East Africa (2021). Local prices vary significantly by country and import duty.

Hiring Your First Employee: The Numbers That Matter

Your first hire should be a production operator, not an administrator. The owner must move to sales and quality control. In most African markets, the fully loaded cost of one production employee is 1.3â1.6 times the base wage once you add statutory contributions, leave, and a modest bonus. Before hiring, calculate your revenue per employee: if adding one person does not raise monthly output value by at least three times their fully loaded cost, the hire is premature.

Practical rules:

  • Write a one-page job description with measurable outputs (e.g., "produce 400 packs of serviettes per shift").
  • Start on a 3-month probation with a clear review date.
  • Register the employee for statutory deductions from day one â informal arrangements create legal and morale risk as you grow.
  • Train the new hire on quality checks before they touch the machine unsupervised.

Investing in a Semi-Automatic Rewinding Machine

A semi-automatic rewinder converts jumbo reels into finished rolls and is the single highest-leverage machine for most small tissue producers. It typically raises output 2â3Ã versus manual rewinding and improves roll consistency, which is what supermarkets and distributors actually buy. Before purchasing:

  • Confirm a minimum 3-month order pipeline that exceeds your current manual capacity.
  • Check power requirements â many units need stable 3-phase supply; budget for a stabiliser or small generator.
  • Source spare parts and a local technician before the machine arrives. A machine down for three weeks erases the investment case.
  • Negotiate training for at least two staff, so knowledge is not held by one person.

Increasing Production Without Compromising Quality

Speed without consistency loses buyers. The practical quality controls that matter most are grammage (paper weight), roll diameter, perforation strength, and packaging cleanliness. Introduce a simple batch log: date, reel supplier, machine settings, output count, and any defects. When a buyer complains, the log tells you whether the problem is the reel or the machine setting.

Table 2: Quality parameters to monitor during scale-up
Parameter Target range Check frequency Common failure cause
Grammage (tissue) 14â18 gsm (toilet), 18â22 gsm (kitchen) Per reel batch Inconsistent jumbo reel supply
Roll diameter Within Â±2 mm of spec Every 30 minutes Worn cutting blade or tension drift
Perforation strength Tears cleanly without shredding Every hour Blunt perforation wheel
Pack count accuracy 100% match to label Every pack Manual counting fatigue
Moisture content < 8% Daily Humid storage without ventilation

Sources: Ranges adapted from ISO 12625 series (tissue paper product standards) and from the Kenya Bureau of Standards KS EAS 855:2019 specification for toilet tissue. Local standards may differ; always check your national bureau of standards.

Finding Larger Buyers: Supermarkets and Distributors

Supermarkets and distributors buy on three criteria: consistent quality, reliable delivery, and credit terms they can manage. They will ask for: business registration, tax compliance certificate, product samples, and a price list. Prepare a one-page supplier pack with these documents plus references from two existing customers. Expect 30â60 day payment terms; you must have working capital to survive the gap between delivery and payment.

Distributors are often easier to reach than supermarket head offices and can give you regional reach. Start with one distributor in your city, deliver flawlessly for three months, then approach the second. Do not chase five distributors at once â service failures will end all of them.

Expanding to New Products: Paper Plates, Cups, and Tissues

New products should be demand-led, not equipment-led. The right trigger is when existing buyers ask for the product, or when you can identify a specific institutional segment (caterers, events, clinics) you already serve. Paper plates and cups require different machinery from tissue and different raw materials, so treat them as a separate business line with its own costing. Run a small trial batch, sell it to existing customers, and only then invest in dedicated equipment.

Financing Growth: Loans, Savings Groups, and Grants

Match the finance to the asset. Working capital (reels, packaging, wages) should come from short-term sources; machinery should come from medium-term loans or grants. In many African markets, the practical ladder is:

  • Internal cash flow â the cheapest capital; build a reserve equal to one month's operating costs.
  • Savings groups / SACCOs / VSLA â accessible, low documentation, good for working capital and small equipment.
  • Bank SME loans â require records; use for machinery with clear payback.
  • Grants and development programmes â competitive; best for training, certification, or piloting new products, not for routine operations.
â  SAFETY WARNING â Machine Operations

Rewinding, cutting, and perforating machines cause serious hand and arm injuries. Never allow operation without a fixed guard over the cutting and perforation area. Isolate power before any blade change, jam clearance, or maintenance. Provide cut-resistant gloves and eye protection, and enforce a no-loose-clothing rule. Train every operator on emergency stop locations before their first unsupervised shift. Report and investigate every near-miss â they predict the next injury.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Demand first: Do not hire or buy equipment until you have three consecutive months of demand exceeding current capacity.
  2. Revenue per employee: A new hire must generate at least 3Ã their fully loaded cost in output value.
  3. Machine readiness: Confirm power supply, spare parts, and a trained local technician before the machine arrives.
  4. Batch log: Record reel supplier, settings, output, and defects for every production batch.
  5. Supplier pack: Keep registration, tax certificate, samples, price list, and two references ready for buyers.
  6. Cash buffer: Maintain at least one month of operating costs before taking on supermarket credit terms.
  7. Finance match: Short-term finance for working capital, medium-term loans or grants for machinery.
  8. Safety first: Guards on, power isolated for maintenance, protective equipment worn, near-misses reported.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • ILO â Growing Your Business: A Handbook for Small and Medium Enterprises (free PDF; practical SME growth stages).
  • African Development Bank â Africa SME Programme (financing and upgrading resources).
  • ISO 12625 series â Tissue paper and tissue products (international quality standards).
  • Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS) â national tissue and paper product specifications (adapt for your country's bureau of standards).
  • FAO â Small-scale Papermaking (free technical reference on paper production).

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills course Tissues & Paper Products. Figures and thresholds are indicative; always verify current prices, standards, and regulations in your country before committing capital.

quiz.q: What is a good rule to know you can afford to hire your first employee?
options: A) When you have more orders than you can fill in a 40-hour week and your profit after materials is at least 3 times the daily wage of a helper
B) When you have been in business for at least 5 years
C) When you have saved 1 million shillings
D) When your competitor hires someone
quiz.explanation: This ensures you can pay a helper and still make a profit.

quiz.q: In Kenya, what is the approximate minimum monthly wage for a general worker as mentioned in the lesson?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states about 15,000 KES per month for a general worker in 2023.

quiz.q: What is one recommended way to find your first employee?
options: A) Post on international job boards
B) Ask family, church, or local Facebook groups
D) Wait for someone to walk in
quiz.explanation: These local networks are practical and often yield reliable candidates.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid hiring friends unless you can be clear about expectations?
options: A) Friends always ask for higher pay
B) It can damage the friendship if you need to correct or fire them
D) Friends will steal from you
quiz.explanation: Mixing friendship and business can lead to personal conflict.

quiz.q: What is a semi-automatic rewinding machine used for?
options: B) Turning jumbo rolls into finished toilet rolls or kitchen towels
quiz.explanation: It converts large jumbo rolls into smaller consumer rolls.

quiz.q: What is the approximate production rate of a semi-automatic rewinding machine compared to manual rewinding?
options: A) 50 rolls per hour vs 200-300 rolls per hour
B) 200-300 rolls per hour vs 50 rolls per hour
C) 500 rolls per hour vs 100 rolls per hour
D) 1000 rolls per hour vs 200 rolls per hour
quiz.explanation: Semi-automatic machines produce 200-300 rolls per hour, while manual does about 50.

quiz.q: What is the typical cost of a used semi-automatic rewinding machine in Africa?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states used machines cost 1.5 to 3 million shillings.

quiz.q: What additional equipment is needed for a semi-automatic rewinding machine?
options: A) A compressor and power stabilizer
B) A generator and water tank
quiz.explanation: The machine requires air pressure and stable power.

quiz.q: What is the recommended space for a semi-automatic rewinding machine?
quiz.explanation: The lesson suggests a dry, secure room at least 3m x 4m.

quiz.q: What is a key maintenance task for a semi-automatic rewinding machine?
options: A) Replacing the motor every month
B) Daily oiling, cleaning glue rollers, and checking cutting blade
D) Running it without load for an hour
quiz.explanation: These tasks keep the machine running smoothly and prevent defects.

quiz.q: What is a good way to maintain quality when increasing production?
options: A) Use cheaper raw materials to save money
B) Standardize your process and use a checklist
C) Skip quality checks to save time
D) Hire more workers without training
quiz.explanation: Standardization ensures consistency even at higher volumes.

quiz.q: What should you check on a finished toilet paper roll?
options: B) Roll weight, perforation, and wrapper tightness
C) Number of sheets per roll
quiz.explanation: These are key quality indicators mentioned in the lesson.

quiz.q: How often should you weigh random rolls for quality control?
options: D) Only when a customer complains
quiz.explanation: Regular checks catch issues early.

quiz.q: What is a recommended maximum waste percentage when increasing production?
quiz.explanation: If more than 5% of rolls are rejected, slow down.

quiz.q: Why is consistency important for supermarket buyers?
options: A) They want every pack to have the same number of rolls and look
B) They prefer variety in packaging
C) They don't care about quality
D) They only buy the cheapest product
quiz.explanation: Supermarkets need uniform products for shelf display and customer trust.

quiz.q: What is a barcode used for in packaging?
options: A) To make the product look modern
B) To allow supermarkets to scan and track inventory
D) To indicate the manufacturing date
quiz.explanation: Barcodes are essential for retail checkout and inventory systems.

quiz.q: Where can you get a barcode in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: GS1 Kenya issues barcodes for products.

quiz.q: What is a good strategy when approaching a supermarket for the first time?
options: A) Demand a large order immediately
B) Offer a trial supply on consignment
C) Offer the lowest price in the market
quiz.explanation: A trial reduces risk for the buyer and helps you prove quality.

quiz.q: What margin should you offer distributors?
quiz.explanation: This margin motivates them to sell your products.

quiz.q: What is a common payment term from supermarkets?
quiz.explanation: Supermarkets often pay within 30 days, so you need working capital.

quiz.q: What raw material is needed for making paper plates?
quiz.explanation: Paper plates are made from food-grade paper board.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost of a manual paper plate machine?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states a manual machine costs 500,000-1,000,000 shillings.

quiz.q: What is a key market for paper cups?
quiz.explanation: These businesses use paper cups for events and water.

quiz.q: What is a good first step before buying a machine for a new product?
options: B) Test the market by asking potential customers
C) Borrow money from a loan shark
quiz.explanation: Market testing reduces the risk of investing in a product that won't sell.

quiz.q: Why should you keep separate records for each product?
options: A) To know which product is profitable
C) To make tax filing harder
quiz.explanation: Separate records help you make informed decisions about each product line.

quiz.q: What is the cheapest source of financing for growth?
options: C) Your own savings and reinvested profit
quiz.explanation: Using your own money avoids interest and debt.

quiz.q: How much of your monthly profit should you aim to save?
quiz.explanation: Saving 20% builds capital for growth.

quiz.q: What is a savings group (chama) and how can it help?
options: A) A group of friends who meet to socialize
B) A group where members contribute monthly and can borrow multiples of their contribution
C) A government program for free money
D) A bank account with high interest
quiz.explanation: Chamas provide accessible loans for small businesses.

quiz.q: What interest rate might a bank charge for an SME loan?
quiz.explanation: Bank loans typically range from 12-18% annually.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid loan sharks (shylocks)?
options: B) They charge very high interest (e.g., 20% per month) that can destroy your business
C) They only lend to large businesses
quiz.explanation: Exorbitant interest rates make repayment impossible for most small businesses.
